paper.title: When Is Tracking Affordable? A Movement-Budget Feasibility Threshold for Dynamic Regret
paper.abstract:
Abstract Dynamic regret measures an online learner against a moving comparator, and
standard analyses assume the learner may move freely at every round.
We study what happens when it may not: the learner is given a hard budget S S on its total movement ∑ t ‖ x t − x t − 1 ‖ \sum_{t}\|x_{t}-x_{t-1}\| .
Our main result is that a movement budget creates a feasibility barrier.
On a domain of diameter D D with G G -Lipschitz convex losses, for every
comparator path length P T ∈ [ D , D ​ T ] P_{T}\in[D,DT] we exhibit a deterministic adversary
that forces R d = Ω ⁡ ( G ​ D ​ T ) R_{d}=\Omega(GDT) on every budget-feasible algorithm whenever S ≤ c ​ P T S\leq cP_{T} for a universal
constant c > 0 c>0 .
This barrier is caused by the budget rather than by a volatile environment:
for fixed D D , it applies when P T = o ⁡ ( T ) P_{T}=o(T) , where the unconstrained minimax rate Θ ⁡ ( G ​ D ⁡ ( D + P T ) ​ T ) \Theta(G\sqrt{D(D+P_{T})T}) is sublinear, so the same instances are learnable
with an unbounded budget and unlearnable without one.
Conversely, projected online gradient descent with a budget-aware step size is
budget-feasible and attains o ⁡ ( G ​ D ​ T ) o(GDT) once S = ω ⁡ ( D + P T ) S=\omega(D+P_{T}) .
Thus the critical movement scale is D + P T D+P_{T} : linear regret is unavoidable
below a sufficiently small constant multiple of P T P_{T} , while sublinear regret
is achievable when S / ( D + P T ) → ∞ S/(D+P_{T})\to\infty in the learnable regime.
The construction rests on a distinction we make explicit: what makes a
comparator expensive to track under a movement budget is the distance it
forces the learner to travel, not its path length.
Above the threshold we give a budget-dependent upper bound and identify the
tight minimax rate in this region as an open problem rather than claiming a
product law.
Experiments support the predicted transition location and the 1 / S 1/S decay.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Dynamic regret in online convex optimization compares a learner’s decisions x t x_{t} to a moving comparator u t u_{t} ( Zinkevich, 2003 ; Hazan, 2016 ) . Without movement constraints, the key quantity is the comparator path length P T = ∑ t ≥ 2 ‖ u t − u t − 1 ‖ P_{T}=\sum_{t\geq 2}\|u_{t}-u_{t-1}\| : over convex G G -Lipschitz losses on a set of diameter D D , the minimax rate is Θ ⁡ ( G ​ D ⁡ ( D + P T ) ​ T ) \Theta(G\sqrt{D(D+P_{T})T}) ( Zinkevich, 2003 ; Besbes et al., 2015 ) , which is sublinear whenever P T = o ⁡ ( D ​ T ) P_{T}=o(DT) . These guarantees treat movement as free. In temporal systems, however, adaptation is often an intervention: reconfiguring a controller, changing a served configuration, or rebalancing a portfolio consumes a limited resource. We impose a hard budget SC = ∑ t ≥ 2 ‖ x t − x t − 1 ‖ ≤ S \mathrm{SC}=\sum_{t\geq 2}\|x_{t}-x_{t-1}\|\leq S and ask when sublinear dynamic regret is feasible at all. Our main point is that path length alone is not the right hardness measure under a movement budget. A random-walk comparator can have large path length while staying spatially concentrated, so a nearly static learner may still do well. The hard case is different: the comparator must force the learner to travel across the domain. We capture this with a deterministic full-range square wave that alternates between the endpoints of the decision set. The learner knows the sequence; the obstruction is purely whether it can afford to move. Theorem 1 gives the resulting feasibility statement. For every P T ∈ [ D , D ​ T ] P_{T}\in[D,DT] , the square-wave instance forces R d = Ω ⁡ ( G ​ D ​ T ) R_{d}=\Omega(GDT) on every learner with S ≤ c ​ P T S\leq cP_{T} , for a universal constant c > 0 c>0 . Conversely, projected OGD with a budget-aware step size is feasible and achieves o ⁡ ( G ​ D ​ T ) o(GDT) once S = ω ⁡ ( D + P T ) S=\omega(D+P_{T}) . Thus a hard movement budget can make tracking impossible even when, for fixed D D and P T = o ⁡ ( T ) P_{T}=o(T) , the unconstrained problem is learnable. Appendix A gives budget-dependent rates above the threshold, experiments, related work, limitations, and full proofs.

sections.heading: Protocol.
sections.text: Fix a horizon T T and a compact convex decision set 𝒦 ⊂ ℝ d \mathcal{K}\subset\mathbb{R}^{d} with diameter D = sup x , y ∈ 𝒦 ‖ x − y ‖ D=\sup_{x,y\in\mathcal{K}}\|x-y\| . At each round t = 1 , … , T t=1,\dots,T the learner selects x t ∈ 𝒦 x_{t}\in\mathcal{K} , then observes a convex loss f t : 𝒦 → ℝ f_{t}:\mathcal{K}\to\mathbb{R} that is G G -Lipschitz, and incurs f t ​ ( x t ) f_{t}(x_{t}) . All norms are Euclidean.

sections.heading: Comparator and path length.
sections.text: A comparator sequence is any { u t } t = 1 T ⊂ 𝒦 \{u_{t}\}_{t=1}^{T}\subset\mathcal{K} ; we take u t ∈ arg ⁡ min x ∈ 𝒦 ​ f t ​ ( x ) u_{t}\in\arg\min_{x\in\mathcal{K}}f_{t}(x) unless stated otherwise. Its path length is P T = ∑ t = 2 T ‖ u t − u t − 1 ‖ , P_{T}\;=\;\sum_{t=2}^{T}\|u_{t}-u_{t-1}\|, (1) which measures how far the comparator travels in total. Note P T P_{T} can be large while the comparator stays in a small region; this range-versus-path distinction is what motivates the full-range construction below.

sections.text: Dynamic regret and switching cost are R d = ∑ t = 1 T [ f t ​ ( x t ) − f t ​ ( u t ) ] , SC = ∑ t = 2 T ‖ x t − x t − 1 ‖ . R_{d}\;=\;\sum_{t=1}^{T}\big[f_{t}(x_{t})-f_{t}(u_{t})\big],\qquad\mathrm{SC}\;=\;\sum_{t=2}^{T}\|x_{t}-x_{t-1}\|. (2) We call an algorithm budget-feasible for budget S S if it guarantees SC ≤ S \mathrm{SC}\leq S on every loss sequence. Throughout, “linear” regret means R d = Ω ⁡ ( G ​ D ​ T ) R_{d}=\Omega(GDT) and “sublinear” means R d = o ⁡ ( G ​ D ​ T ) R_{d}=o(GDT) ; the normalization by G ​ D GD is natural because | f t ​ ( x ) − f t ​ ( y ) | ≤ G ​ ‖ x − y ‖ ≤ G ​ D |f_{t}(x)-f_{t}(y)|\leq G\|x-y\|\leq GD gives the trivial bound R d ≤ G ​ D ​ T R_{d}\leq GDT for any learner.

sections.heading: Unconstrained benchmark.
sections.text: Without a budget, the minimax dynamic regret is Θ ⁡ ( G ​ D ⁡ ( D + P T ) ​ T ) \Theta(G\sqrt{D(D+P_{T})T}) ( Zinkevich, 2003 ; Besbes et al., 2015 ) , and projected online gradient descent attains it. This is o ⁡ ( G ​ D ​ T ) o(GDT) precisely when P T = o ⁡ ( D ​ T ) P_{T}=o(DT) . For fixed D D , the regime P T = o ⁡ ( T ) P_{T}=o(T) therefore matters for us: it is where the unconstrained problem is learnable, and hence where any impossibility result can be attributed to the budget rather than to the environment.

sections.heading: The budgeted problem.
sections.text: Given S S , we ask for which S S some budget-feasible algorithm achieves R d = o ⁡ ( G ​ D ​ T ) R_{d}=o(GDT) , and what rate is attainable when one does.

sections.heading: 3 The Movement-Budget Feasibility Threshold
sections.text: Path length can overstate hardness under a movement budget: a random-walk comparator has path length Θ ⁡ ( T ​ σ ) \Theta(T\sigma) but range only Θ ⁡ ( σ ​ T ) \Theta(\sigma\sqrt{T}) , so it need not force the learner to travel far. We instead use a deterministic full-range comparator. Let 𝒦 = [ 0 , D ] \mathcal{K}=[0,D] and f t ​ ( x ) = G ​ | x − u t | f_{t}(x)=G|x-u_{t}| . For a target P T ∈ [ D , D ​ T ] P_{T}\in[D,DT] , choose n = min ⁡ { ⌊ P T / D ⌋ , T − 1 } n=\min\{\lfloor P_{T}/D\rfloor,T-1\} endpoint crossings and let u t u_{t} alternate between 0 0 and D D in n + 1 n+1 long blocks. The realized path length is at most P T P_{T} , and the learner knows the comparator exactly; the only obstacle is whether it can afford the crossings. Theorem 1 (Movement-budget feasibility threshold) . Fix a horizon T T , a domain of diameter D D , and a path length P T P_{T} with D ≤ P T ≤ D ​ T D\leq P_{T}\leq DT . 1. (Impossibility.) There exist universal constants c 0 , c 1 > 0 c_{0},c_{1}>0 such that for every algorithm with SC ≤ S \mathrm{SC}\leq S there is a comparator sequence of path length at most P T P_{T} and a sequence of convex, G G -Lipschitz losses on which R d ≥ c 0 ​ G ​ D ​ T ​ ( 1 − c 1 ​ S P T ) . R_{d}\;\geq\;c_{0}GDT\left(1-c_{1}\frac{S}{P_{T}}\right). (3) In particular R d = Ω ⁡ ( G ​ D ​ T ) R_{d}=\Omega(GDT) whenever S ≤ c ​ P T S\leq cP_{T} for a sufficiently small universal constant c > 0 c>0 . 2. (Achievability.) sections.heading: 4 Rates Above the Threshold and Evidence
sections.text: The feasibility theorem answers when sublinear regret is possible. Above that threshold, the finer rate is only partially characterized. Running projected OGD with η = min ⁡ { D ⁡ ( D + 2 ​ P T ) G 2 ​ T , S G ​ T } \eta=\min\!\left\{\sqrt{\frac{D(D+2P_{T})}{G^{2}T}},\frac{S}{GT}\right\} keeps SC ≤ S \mathrm{SC}\leq S and gives R d ≤ O ⁡ ( min ⁡ { G ​ D ⁡ ( D + 2 ​ P T ) ​ T + G ​ T ​ D ​ ( D + 2 ​ P T ) S , G ​ D ​ T } ) . R_{d}\leq O\!\left(\min\left\{G\sqrt{D(D+2P_{T})T}+\frac{GTD(D+2P_{T})}{S},\,GDT\right\}\right). (5) The first term is the usual unconstrained OGD rate; the second is the price of shrinking the step size to fit the movement budget. The standard unconstrained lower bound Ω ⁡ ( G ​ D ​ P T ​ T ) \Omega(G\sqrt{DP_{T}T}) ( Besbes et al., 2015 ) still applies, but we do not claim a matching lower bound for the budget-dependent 1 / S 1/S term. Determining the minimax rate above the feasibility threshold remains open. Our experiments are designed around this separation. Figure 1 tests the theorem itself: the left panel shows the transition as S / P T S/P_{T} varies, while the right panel fixes P T = T = o ⁡ ( T ) P_{T}=\sqrt{T}=o(T) and separates a budget-induced barrier from ordinary nonstationarity. Appendix D reports two further checks. First, random-walk and rotating-comparator experiments show an empirical 1 / S 1/S decay consistent with the upper bound ( 5 ), but we do not treat this as proof that the 1 / S 1/S term is minimax tight. Second, five real daily series, S&P 500, EUR/USD, crude oil via USO, Bitcoin, and New York City temperature, show regret remaining high for S ≪ P T S\ll P_{T} and dropping near S = P T S=P_{T} . These finite-horizon experiments test transition location and budget–regret behavior; asymptotic linearity is certified by the square-wave construction, not by the real series. The closest prior work studies adjacent but different questions. Classical dynamic-regret results characterize adaptation to a moving comparator when movement is free ( Zinkevich, 2003 ; Besbes et al., 2015 ) , with later work removing prior knowledge of P T P_{T} or improving constants in richer loss classes ( Yang et al., 2016 ; Baby and Wang, 2021 ; Zhao et al., 2024 ) . Smoothed online optimization penalizes movement with a Lagrange multiplier rather than imposing a hard budget ( Lin et al., 2011 ; Andrew et al., 2013 ; Chen et al., 2018 ; Goel et al., 2019 ; Zhang et al., 2021 ) . Hard switching-budget work is closest in spirit, but existing results focus on static regret or switching count rather than a distance budget for dynamic regret ( Dekel et al., 2014 ; Chen et al., 2020 ; Sherman and Koren, 2021 ; Wang et al., 2021 ) . Our contribution is the feasibility barrier: even when unconstrained dynamic regret is sublinear, a hard movement budget below the scale D + P T D+P_{T} can make tracking impossible. This perspective is useful for temporal systems because it separates two roles often conflated under the term “adaptation.” Prediction asks whether the learner can infer where the moving optimum is; intervention asks whether the learner can afford to move there. The square-wave construction removes the prediction issue entirely: the comparator is deterministic and known, yet the learner still fails when its movement budget is too small. Thus the threshold is not a statistical limitation but a physical or operational one. The remaining gap is also conceptually sharp. Below the threshold, range forces a feasibility barrier. Far above it, standard OGD rates reappear. In between, the known upper bound has a 1 / S 1/S term, but no matching budget-dependent lower bound is known. Deciding whether this term is an OGD artifact or an unavoidable cost is the main technical question left by the paper.

sections.heading: Appendix A Additional Rates, Experiments, and Discussion
sections.text: We state this as a threshold in scale and not as a sharp threshold with a determined constant, and the distinction is real. The impossibility bound ( 3 ) has only universal-constant precision, while the experiments in Section D.1 indicate that the empirical transition is close to S = P T S=P_{T} . Section D.1 reports the empirical constant separately from the proved one, and we do not conflate them.

R_{d}\;\leq\;O\!\left(\min\left\{G\sqrt{D(D+2P_{T})T}+\frac{GTD(D+2P_{T})}{S},\;\;GDT\right\}\right). sections.heading: Appendix C Budget-Controlled OGD

(7) Proposition 4 (Budget-Controlled OGD) . Assume each f t f_{t} is convex and G G -Lipschitz. The update ( 7 ) satisfies SC ≤ S \mathrm{SC}\leq S and 𝔼 ⁡ [ R d ] ≤ O ⁡ ( G ​ D ⁡ ( D + 2 ​ P T ) ​ T + G ​ T ​ D ​ ( D + 2 ​ P T ) / S ) \mathbb{E}[R_{d}]\leq O\!\big(G\sqrt{D(D+2P_{T})T}+GTD(D+2P_{T})/S\big) . When P T P_{T} is unknown, a doubling trick preserves the rate up to constants. The algorithm is not new: it is the standard OGD of Zinkevich [2003] run at a particular step size. What the analysis contributes is the identification of that step size. The two arguments of the minimum in ( 7 ) correspond to the two regimes: the first is the usual unconstrained optimum, the second is the largest step for which the budget is respected without any explicit projection onto the constraint, since per-round movement is bounded by η ​ G \eta G and there are T T rounds. Budget feasibility is thus enforced by the step size alone. We do not claim ( 7 ) is a new optimization method, and by Remark 3 we use it as a constructive upper bound rather than as a fully minimax-optimal method above the threshold.

sections.heading: D.4 Algorithm comparison
sections.text: Across oscillating, rotating, and piecewise stationary synthetic environments, Budget-Controlled OGD matches or outperforms Lazy OGD, SOCO, and Periodic Restart at all budget levels (Appendix K , Figure 7 ); Periodic Restart is included as a standard baseline for non-stationary online optimization [ Besbes et al., 2015 ] . Lazy OGD is handicapped by its threshold update rule, which spends budget on small moves during low-volatility stretches; Periodic Restart suffers when its restart boundaries are misaligned with the environment. On real data the same ordering holds on the S&P 500, Bitcoin, and NYC temperature series.

sections.heading: D.5 Real-world series
sections.text: We use five daily series as comparator sequences, each normalized: the S&P 500 index ( T = 1509 T{=}1509 ), the EUR/USD exchange rate ( T = 1564 T{=}1564 ), crude oil via the USO ETF ( T = 1509 T{=}1509 ), Bitcoin ( T = 2191 T{=}2191 ), and mean temperature in New York City ( T = 2192 T{=}2192 ). sections.heading: Dynamic regret.
sections.text: Dynamic regret against a moving comparator originates with Zinkevich [2003] , who gave the O ⁡ ( D ⁡ ( D + P T ) / η + η ​ G 2 ​ T ) O(D(D+P_{T})/\eta+\eta G^{2}T) bound for OGD that we use. Besbes et al. [2015] established minimax rates for non-stationary stochastic optimization and supply the Ω ⁡ ( G ​ D ​ P T ​ T ) \Omega(G\sqrt{DP_{T}T}) lower bound in Theorem 2 . Subsequent work develops adaptive and parameter-free methods that attain path-length-dependent rates without knowing P T P_{T} [ Yang et al., 2016 , Zhang et al., 2018 , Zhao et al., 2020 , Baby and Wang, 2021 , Zhao et al., 2024 ] , and Jacobsen and Orabona [2024] relates static and dynamic regret through lifted constructions. All of this assumes movement is free.

sections.heading: Switching costs and smoothed online optimization.
sections.text: Smoothed online convex optimization augments the loss with a movement penalty, ∑ t f t ​ ( x t ) + λ ​ ∑ t ‖ x t − x t − 1 ‖ \sum_{t}f_{t}(x_{t})+\lambda\sum_{t}\|x_{t}-x_{t-1}\| , and yields competitive algorithms such as online balanced descent [ Lin et al., 2011 , Andrew et al., 2013 , Chen et al., 2018 , Goel et al., 2019 ] . Recent work also studies dynamic regret when the switching cost is part of the performance metric [ Zhang et al., 2021 ] . A soft penalty selects a single operating point through λ \lambda ; it does not answer whether learning is possible at a prescribed budget, which is the question Theorem 1 addresses.

sections.heading: Hard switching constraints.
sections.text: Closest to our setting are hard constraints on movement. Wang et al. [2021] study continuous switching distance constraints and Sherman and Koren [2021] constrain the switching count ; both target static regret. Switching-budget lower bounds also appear in bandit and switching-constrained OCO models [ Dekel et al., 2014 , Chen et al., 2020 ] . Table 1 summarizes the positioning. To our knowledge no prior work identifies a feasibility threshold for dynamic regret under a hard movement-distance budget. The exact minimax rate above that threshold remains open (Remark 3 ).

sections.heading: Rates above the threshold.
sections.text: The main open problem is the minimax rate once S S exceeds the feasibility threshold. Resolving it appears to require understanding whether the 1 / S 1/S term in Theorem 2 is an OGD artifact or reflects an unavoidable budget-dependent price. The two natural lower-bound constructions each fail on one count. Our square wave is deterministic and becomes exactly trackable once S ≥ P T S\geq P_{T} , so it certifies nothing above the threshold. A drifting comparator can be followed with O ⁡ ( P T ) O(P_{T}) additional movement once the observed losses reveal its position, so for S ≫ P T S\gg P_{T} increasing P T P_{T} does not obviously help the adversary. We therefore do not claim minimax optimality for Theorem 2 .

sections.heading: The constant in the threshold.
sections.text: Theorem 1 proves the threshold only up to universal constants, while the exact dynamic program of Section D.1 indicates the empirical transition is close to S = P T S=P_{T} . The result should therefore be read as identifying the asymptotic movement scale D + P T D+P_{T} , not as determining the exact constant-factor transition. The slack is localized to inequality ( 11 ).

sections.heading: What each piece of evidence supports.
sections.text: We distinguish three levels deliberately. The square-wave construction proves linear regret for S ≤ c ​ P T S\leq cP_{T} for a universal constant c > 0 c>0 , uniformly over P T ∈ [ D , D ​ T ] P_{T}\in[D,DT] , and Figure 2 (B) provides the corresponding empirical demonstration at P T = o ⁡ ( T ) P_{T}=o(T) . The random-walk and real-data experiments show that the transition sits near S = P T S=P_{T} and that regret decays as 1 / S 1/S ; because they run at fixed finite horizons they cannot distinguish Θ ⁡ ( T ) \Theta(T) from o ⁡ ( T ) o(T) , and because the random-walk comparator is spatially concentrated it could not certify a budget-induced barrier even asymptotically. The tight rate above the threshold, and the exact constant at the threshold, remain unknown .

sections.heading: Other limitations.
sections.text: The lower bound is one-dimensional; it lifts to ℝ d \mathbb{R}^{d} by embedding, but the dimension dependence of the constants is not resolved. Our synthetic non-square-wave experiments use quadratic losses, while the theory covers all convex Lipschitz losses. We assume full gradient feedback; we note that the square-wave argument is information-free, so it may transfer to bandit feedback directly, though we have not verified this.

sections.heading: Appendix G Conclusion
sections.text: A hard movement budget can make dynamic tracking impossible even when the underlying non-stationarity is mild enough that unconstrained dynamic regret is sublinear. Concretely: a deterministic full-range adversary forces linear regret on every budget-feasible algorithm whenever S ≤ c ​ P T S\leq cP_{T} for a universal constant c > 0 c>0 and every P T ∈ [ D , D ​ T ] P_{T}\in[D,DT] ; projected OGD with a budget-aware step size achieves o ⁡ ( G ​ D ​ T ) o(GDT) once S = ω ⁡ ( D + P T ) S=\omega(D+P_{T}) ; together these identify D + P T D+P_{T} as the critical movement scale, with the constant-factor band left open. Above the threshold, budget-controlled OGD gives a concrete 1 / S 1/S upper bound, but its minimax tightness remains open. Experiments support the transition picture, locate it near S = P T S=P_{T} , and exhibit empirical 1 / S 1/S decay. The construction turns on treating comparator range rather than path length as the relevant measure of difficulty, and we expect that distinction to be useful wherever a learner is charged for the distance it travels.

A Movement-Budget Feasibility Threshold for Dynamic Regret Ridham Patel Affiliation: Computer Science & Engineering Affiliation: Indian Institute of Technology Gandhinagar Affiliation: Gandhinagar, India Email: ridham.patel@iitgn.ac.in Abstract Dynamic regret measures an online learner against a moving comparator, and standard analyses assume the learner may move freely at every round. We study what happens when it may not: the learner is given a hard budget S S on its total movement ∑ t ‖ x t − x t − 1 ‖ \sum_{t}\|x_{t}-x_{t-1}\| . Our main result is that a movement budget creates a feasibility barrier. On a domain of diameter D D with G G -Lipschitz convex losses, for every comparator path length P T ∈ [ D , D ​ T ] P_{T}\in[D,DT] we exhibit a deterministic adversary that forces R d = Ω ⁡ ( G ​ D ​ T ) R_{d}=\Omega(GDT) on every budget-feasible algorithm whenever S ≤ c ​ P T S\leq cP_{T} for a universal constant c > 0 c>0 . This barrier is caused by the budget rather than by a volatile environment: for fixed D D , it applies when P T = o ⁡ ( T ) P_{T}=o(T) , where the unconstrained minimax rate Θ ⁡ ( G ​ D ⁡ ( D + P T ) ​ T ) \Theta(G\sqrt{D(D+P_{T})T}) is sublinear, so the same instances are learnable with an unbounded budget and unlearnable without one. Conversely, projected online gradient descent with a budget-aware step size is budget-feasible and attains o ⁡ ( G ​ D ​ T ) o(GDT) once S = ω ⁡ ( D + P T ) S=\omega(D+P_{T}) . Thus the critical movement scale is D + P T D+P_{T} : linear regret is unavoidable below a sufficiently small constant multiple of P T P_{T} , while sublinear regret is achievable when S / ( D + P T ) → ∞ S/(D+P_{T})\to\infty in the learnable regime. The construction rests on a distinction we make explicit: what makes a comparator expensive to track under a movement budget is the distance it forces the learner to travel, not its path length. Above the threshold we give a budget-dependent upper bound and identify the tight minimax rate in this region as an open problem rather than claiming a product law. Experiments support the predicted transition location and the 1 / S 1/S decay. 1 Introduction Dynamic regret in online convex optimization compares a learner’s decisions x t x_{t} to a moving comparator u t u_{t} ( Zinkevich, 2003 ; Hazan, 2016 ) . Without movement constraints, the key quantity is the comparator path length P T = ∑ t ≥ 2 ‖ u t − u t − 1 ‖ P_{T}=\sum_{t\geq 2}\|u_{t}-u_{t-1}\| : over convex G G -Lipschitz losses on a set of diameter D D , the minimax rate is Θ ⁡ ( G ​ D ⁡ ( D + P T ) ​ T ) \Theta(G\sqrt{D(D+P_{T})T}) ( Zinkevich, 2003 ; Besbes et al., 2015 ) , which is sublinear whenever P T = o ⁡ ( D ​ T ) P_{T}=o(DT) . These guarantees treat movement as free. In temporal systems, however, adaptation is often an intervention: reconfiguring a controller, changing a served configuration, or rebalancing a portfolio consumes a limited resource. We impose a hard budget SC = ∑ t ≥ 2 ‖ x t − x t − 1 ‖ ≤ S \mathrm{SC}=\sum_{t\geq 2}\|x_{t}-x_{t-1}\|\leq S and ask when sublinear dynamic regret is feasible at all. Our main point is that path length alone is not the right hardness measure under a movement budget. A random-walk comparator can have large path length while staying spatially concentrated, so a nearly static learner may still do well. The hard case is different: the comparator must force the learner to travel across the domain. We capture this with a deterministic full-range square wave that alternates between the endpoints of the decision set. The learner knows the sequence; the obstruction is purely whether it can afford to move. Theorem 1 gives the resulting feasibility statement. For every P T ∈ [ D , D ​ T ] P_{T}\in[D,DT] , the square-wave instance forces R d = Ω ⁡ ( G ​ D ​ T ) R_{d}=\Omega(GDT) on every learner with S ≤ c ​ P T S\leq cP_{T} , for a universal constant c > 0 c>0 . Conversely, projected OGD with a budget-aware step size is feasible and achieves o ⁡ ( G ​ D ​ T ) o(GDT) once S = ω ⁡ ( D + P T ) S=\omega(D+P_{T}) . Thus a hard movement budget can make tracking impossible even when, for fixed D D and P T = o ⁡ ( T ) P_{T}=o(T) , the unconstrained problem is learnable. These finite-horizon experiments test transition location and budget–regret behavior; asymptotic linearity is certified by the square-wave construction, not by the real series. The closest prior work studies adjacent but different questions. Classical dynamic-regret results characterize adaptation to a moving comparator when movement is free ( Zinkevich, 2003 ; Besbes et al., 2015 ) , with later work removing prior knowledge of P T P_{T} or improving constants in richer loss classes ( Yang et al., 2016 ; Baby and Wang, 2021 ; Zhao et al., 2024 ) . Smoothed online optimization penalizes movement with a Lagrange multiplier rather than imposing a hard budget ( Lin et al., 2011 ; Andrew et al., 2013 ; Chen et al., 2018 ; Goel et al., 2019 ; Zhang et al., 2021 ) . Hard switching-budget work is closest in spirit, but existing results focus on static regret or switching count rather than a distance budget for dynamic regret ( Dekel et al., 2014 ; Chen et al., 2020 ; Sherman and Koren, 2021 ; Wang et al., 2021 ) . Our contribution is the feasibility barrier: even when unconstrained dynamic regret is sublinear, a hard movement budget below the scale D + P T D+P_{T} can make tracking impossible. This perspective is useful for temporal systems because it separates two roles often conflated under the term “adaptation.” Prediction asks whether the learner can infer where the moving optimum is; intervention asks whether the learner can afford to move there. The square-wave construction removes the prediction issue entirely: the comparator is deterministic and known, yet the learner still fails when its movement budget is too small. Thus the threshold is not a statistical limitation but a physical or operational one. The remaining gap is also conceptually sharp. Below the threshold, range forces a feasibility barrier. Far above it, standard OGD rates reappear. In between, the known upper bound has a 1 / S 1/S term, but no matching budget-dependent lower bound is known.
